ul.li: supervise the handling of the material to the point of destruction;
ensure that the destruction is completed successfully;
sign a destruction certificate; and
complete the relevant entries in the destruction register.

group.title: Outsourcing media and IT Equipment destruction

control.title: 13.5.29.C.02. — Outsourcing media and IT Equipment destruction

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Outsourcing media and IT Equipment destruction

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies outsourcing the destruction of media and IT Equipment to a commercial facility MUST use an approved facility and comply with the procedures and instructions in this Chapter.

group.title: Transporting media and IT Equipment for offsite destruction

control.title: 13.5.30.C.01. — Transporting media and IT Equipment for offsite destruction

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Transporting media and IT Equipment for offsite destruction

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD sanitise media and IT Equipment prior to transporting it to an offsite location for destruction.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST declassify all media and IT equipment prior to disposing of it into the public domain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Media and IT equipment that cannot be effectively sanitised or declassified MUST be destroyed and not released into the public domain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST document procedures for the disposal of media and IT equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies declassifying media MUST ensure that:

ul.li: the reclassification of all classified information on the media has been approved by the originator, or the media has been appropriately sanitised or destroyed; and
formal approval is granted before the media is released into the public domain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST dispose of media in a manner that does not draw undue attention to its previous classification.

part.name: statement
part.p: Media and IT equipment that has contained NZEO material MUST be sanitised and redeployed or sanitised and destroyed in accordance with the procedures in this chapter.

part.name: statement
part.p: For disposal of all NZEO endorsed materials, an approved destruction facility MUST be used.

part.name: statement
part.p: Media and IT equipment that has contained NZEO material MUST NOT be disposed of via e-recyclers or sold to any third party.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where agencies establish their own disposal/destruction facilities, these facilities MUST be approved by the Director-General GCSB.

group.title: Use of Approved Secure Destruction Facilities

control.title: 13.6.12.C.01. — Use of Approved Secure Destruction Facilities

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Use of Approved Secure Destruction Facilities

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use an approved secure disposal/destruction facility for the destruction of media and IT equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD develop a hardened SOE for workstations and servers, covering:

ul.li: removal of unneeded software and operating system components;
removal or disabling of unneeded services, ports and BIOS settings;
disabling of unused or undesired functionality in software and operating systems;
implementation of access controls on relevant objects to limit system users and programs to the minimum access required;
installation of antivirus and anti-malware software;
installation of software-based firewalls limiting inbound and outbound network connections;
configuration of either remote logging or the transfer of local event logs to a central server; and
protection of audit and other logs through the use of a one way pipe to reduce likelihood of compromise key transaction records.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that for all servers and workstations:

ul.li: a technical specification is agreed for each platform with specified controls;
a standard configuration created and updated for each operating system type and version;
system users do not have the ability to install or disable software without approval; and
installed software and operating system patching is up to date.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that for all servers and workstations:

ul.li: malware detection heuristics are set to a high level;
malware pattern signatures are checked for updates on at least a daily basis;
malware pattern signatures are updated as soon as possible after vendors make them available;
all disks and systems are regularly scanned for malicious code; and
the use of End Point Agents is considered.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD reduce potential vulnerabilities in their SOEs by:

ul.li: removing unused accounts;
renaming or deleting default accounts; and
replacing default passwords, before or during the installation process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where servers with a high security risk have connectivity to unsecure public networks, agencies SHOULD:

ul.li: use appropriately designed and configured gateways;
consider the use of cross-domain solutions;
segment networks;
maintain effective functional segregation between servers allowing them to operate independently;
minimise communications between servers at both the network and file system level as appropriate; and
limit system users and programs to the minimum access needed to perform their duties.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD:

ul.li: characterise all servers whose functions are critical to the agency, and those identified as being at a high security risk of compromise;
store the characterisation information securely off the server in a manner that maintains integrity;
update the characterisation information after every legitimate change to a system as part of the change control process;

as part of the agency’s ongoing audit schedule, compare the stored characterisation information against current characterisation information to determine whether a compromise, or a legitimate but incorrectly completed system modification, has occurred;
perform the characterisation from a trusted environment rather than the standard operating system wherever possible; and
resolve any detected changes in accordance with the agency’s information security incident management procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use an Approved Cryptographic Algorithm to perform cryptographic checksums for characterisation purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD consider characterisations in the context of a BCP or DRP and any related Business Impact Analyses and Risk Assessments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD review all software applications to determine whether they attempt to establish any unauthorised or unplanned external connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: If automated outbound connection functionality is included, agencies SHOULD make a business decision to determine whether to permit or deny these connections, including an assessment of the security risks involved in doing so.

part.name: statement
part.p: If automated outbound connection functionality is included, agencies SHOULD consider the implementation of Data Loss Prevention (DLP) technologies.

group.title: Knowledge of software used on systems

control.title: 14.1.14.C.01. — Knowledge of software used on systems

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Knowledge of software used on systems

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD limit information that could be disclosed outside the agency about what software, and software versions are installed on their systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement application allow listing as part of the SOE for workstations, servers and any other network device.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that a system user cannot disable the application allow listing mechanism.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD prevent a system user from running arbitrary executables.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD restrict a system user’s rights in order to permit them to only execute a specific set of predefined executables as required for them to complete their duties.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that application allow listing does not replace the antivirus and anti-malware software within a system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that system administrators are not automatically exempt from application allow list policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that the default policy is to deny the execution of software.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that application allow listing is used in addition to a strong access control list model and the use of limited privilege accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD plan and test application allow listing mechanisms and processes thoroughly prior to implementation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD restrict the decision whether to run an executable based on the following, in the order of preference shown:

ul.li: validates cryptographic hash;
executable absolute path;
digital signature; and
parent folder.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD restrict the process creation permissions of any executables which are permitted to run by the application allow listing controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD validate executable behaviour, in particular process creation, permission changes and access control modifications through examination, testing, monitoring and restriction of the permissions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Logs from the application allow listing implementation SHOULD include all relevant information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST develop and implement a policy governing appropriate Web usage.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use a Web proxy for all Web browsing activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: An agency’s Web proxy SHOULD authenticate system users and provide logging that includes at least the following details about websites accessed:

ul.li: address (uniform resource locator);
time/date;
system user;
internal IP address; and
external IP address.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT permit downloading of executable files from external websites unless there is a demonstrable and approved business requirement.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD disable the automatic launching of files downloaded from external websites.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies permitting TLS through their gateways SHOULD implement:

ul.li: a solution that decrypts and inspects the TLS traffic as per content filtering requirements; or
an allow list specifying the addresses (uniform resource locators) to which encrypted connections are permitted, with all other addresses blocked.

group.title: Legal advice on the Inspection of TLS traffic

control.title: 14.3.9.C.01. — Legal advice on the Inspection of TLS traffic

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Legal advice on the Inspection of TLS traffic

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD seek legal advice regarding the inspection of encrypted TLS traffic by their gateways.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement allow listing for all HTTP traffic being communicated through their gateways.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using an allow list on their gateways to specify the external addresses, to which encrypted connections are permitted, SHOULD specify allow list addresses by domain name or IP address.

part.name: statement
part.p: If agencies do not allow list websites they SHOULD deny list websites to prevent access to known malicious websites.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies deny listing websites SHOULD update the deny list on a frequent basis to ensure that it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD block client-side active content, such as Java and ActiveX, which are assessed as having a limited business impact.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD:

ul.li: use client-side controls that allow JavaScript on a per website basis; and
add JavaScript functions used only for malicious purposes to the agency Web content filter or IDS/IPS.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use the Web proxy to filter content that is potentially harmful to system users and their workstations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users MUST NOT use agency userID and login passwords as credentials for external websites.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users SHOULD NOT store web site authentication credentials (userID and password) on workstations, remote access devices (such as laptops) or BYO devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users SHOULD NOT use the same password for multiple websites.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that software development environments are configured such that:

ul.li: there are at least three separate environments covering:
development;
testing; and
production.
information flow between the environments is strictly limited according to a defined and documented change policy, with access granted only to system users with a clear business requirement;
new development and modifications only take place in the development environment; and
write access to the authoritative source for the software (source libraries & production environment) is disabled.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that software developers use secure programming practices when writing code, including:

ul.li: designing software to use the lowest privilege level needed to achieve its task;
denying access by default;
checking return values of all system calls; and
validating all inputs.

part.name: statement
part.p: Software SHOULD be reviewed or tested for vulnerabilities before it is used in a production environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Software SHOULD be reviewed or tested by an independent party as well as the developer.

part.name: statement
part.p: Software development SHOULD follow secure coding practices and agency development standards.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD review all active content on their Web servers for known information security issues.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD minimise connectivity and access between each Web application component.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD follow the documentation provided in the Open Web Application Security Project guide to building secure Web applications and Web services.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST develop and implement a policy governing the use of email.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that emails containing NZEO or other nationality releasability marked information are sent only to named recipients.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT transmit emails or other documents, containing NZEO or other nationality releasability marks, to groups or distribution lists unless the nationality of all members of the distribution lists can be confirmed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD comply with the national classification system for the application of protective markings.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT allow system users to select protective markings that the system has not been accredited to process, store or communicate.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT allow a protective marking to be inserted into system user generated emails without their intervention.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT permit system users replying to or forwarding an email to select a protective marking that indicates that the classification of the email is lower than a previous classification used for the email.

part.name: statement
part.p: All classified and unclassified emails MUST have a protective marking.

part.name: statement
part.p: Email protective markings MUST accurately reflect the highest classification of all elements in an email, including any attachments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD include protective markings in the email subject line or header to facilitate early identification of the classification.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an unmarked email has originated outside the government, the agency MUST assess the information and determine how it is to be handled in accordance with the classification system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an email is of a personal nature and does not contain government information, protective markings SHOULD NOT be used.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an unmarked email has originated from a New Zealand or overseas government agency, personnel SHOULD contact the originator to determine how it is to be handled.

group.title: Receiving emails with unknown protective markings

control.title: 15.1.15.C.01. — Receiving emails with unknown protective markings

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Receiving emails with unknown protective markings

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an email is received with an unknown protective marking from a New Zealand or overseas government agency, personnel SHOULD contact the originator to determine appropriate protection measures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD configure systems so that the protective markings appear at the top and bottom of every page when the email is printed, in CAPITALS and appearing as the first and last item on each page.

part.name: statement
part.p: Personnel SHOULD NOT send emails that contain active Web addresses or click on active Web addresses within emails they receive.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST make their system users aware of the agency’s email usage policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement measures to monitor their personnel’s compliance with email usage policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD enforce the use of approved government email systems such as SEEMAIL.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT allow personnel to use public Web-based email services, for processing, receiving or sending emails or attachments for official business.

group.title: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

control.title: 15.2.36.C.01. — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

part.name: statement
part.p: Before implementing DMARC agencies MUST:

ul.li: Create a DMARC policy;
List all domains, in particular those used for the sending and/or receiving of email;
Review the configuration of SPF and DKIM for all active domains and all published domains; and
Establish one or more monitored inboxes to receive DMARC reports.

control.title: 15.2.36.C.02 — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST enable DMARC with a policy of p=reject for all email originating from or received by their domain(s). See 15.2.16 for a recommended approach where a domain is used for sending and/or receiving email and disruption would cause a business impact.

control.title: 15.2.36.C.03 — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST manage “received DMARC messages” in accordance with the agency’s published DMARC policy.

control.title: 15.2.36.C.04 — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST review DMARC reports on a regular basis and address any identified anomalies or security issues.

control.title: 15.2.36.C.05 — Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC)

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD produce failure reports and aggregate reports according to the agency’s DMARC policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD configure the following gateway filters:

ul.li: inbound and outbound email, including any attachments, that contain:
malicious code;
content in conflict with the agency’s email policy;
content that cannot be identified;
deny listed or unauthorised filetypes; and
encrypted content, when that content cannot be inspected for malicious code or authenticated as originating from a trusted source;
emails addressed to internal-use only email aliases with source addresses located from outside the domain; and
all emails arriving via an external connection where the source address uses an internal agency domain name.

group.title: Active web addresses (URL) embedded in emails

control.title: 15.2.38.C.01 — Active web addresses (URL) embedded in emails

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Active web addresses (URL) embedded in emails

part.name: statement
part.p: Email servers SHOULD be configured to strip active addresses and URL’s and replace them with text only versions.

group.title: Preventing unmarked or inappropriately marked emails

control.title: 15.2.39.C.03 — Preventing unmarked or inappropriately marked emails

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Preventing unmarked or inappropriately marked emails

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD enforce protective marking of emails so that checking and filtering can take place.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST configure systems to block any outbound emails with a protective marking or endorsement indicating that the content of the email exceeds the classification of the communication path.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD configure systems to log every occurrence of a blocked email.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST configure email systems to reject, log and report inbound emails with protective markings indicating that the content of the email exceeds the accreditation of the receiving system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD notify the intended recipient of any blocked emails.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD only send notification of undeliverable, bounced, or blocked emails to senders that can be verified via SPF or other trusted means.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that the requirements for blocking unmarked and outbound emails are also applied to automatically forwarded emails.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST disable open email relaying so that email servers will only relay messages destined for the agency’s domain(s) and those originating from authorised systems or users within that domain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD perform regular email server auditing, security reviews and vulnerability analysis activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an agency has system users that send email from outside the agency’s network, an authenticated and encrypted channel MUST be configured to allow email to be sent via the centralised email gateway.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD route email through a centralised email gateway.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where backup or alternative email gateways are in place, additional email gateways SHOULD be maintained at the same standard as the primary email gateway.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST enable opportunistic TLS encryption as defined in IETF’s RFC 3207 on email servers that make incoming or outgoing email connections over public infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement TLS between email servers where significant volumes of classified information are passed via email to other agencies.

group.title: Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

control.title: 15.2.48.C.01. — Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD enable MTA-STS to prevent the unencrypted transfer of emails between complying servers.

control.title: 15.2.48.C.02. — Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use TLS 1.2 or above when implementing MTA-STS.

control.title: 15.2.48.C.03. — Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Mail transfer agent - strict transfer security

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD enable TLS reporting when implementing MTA-STS.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: specify mail servers using SPF or Sender ID; and
mark, block or identify incoming emails that fail SPF checks for notification to the email recipient.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: use a fail SPF record when specifying email servers; and
use SPF or Sender ID to verify the authenticity of incoming emails.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD refer to the SPF recommendations in IETF’s RFC 7208.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST enable DKIM signing on all email originating from their domain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use DKIM in conjunction with SPF.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD verify DKIM signatures on emails received, taking into account that email distribution list software typically invalidates DKIM signatures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where agencies operate email distribution list software used by external senders, agencies SHOULD configure the software so that it does not impair the validity of the sender’s DKIM signature.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: develop, implement and maintain a set of policies and procedures covering all system users’:
identification;
authentication;
authorisation;
privileged access identification and management; and
make their system users aware of the agency’s policies and procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD design and implement Zero Trust principles and architecture to strengthen identification management.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that all system users are:

ul.li: uniquely identifiable; and
authorised and authenticated on each occasion that access is granted to a system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT use shared credentials to access administrator or privileged access accounts.
NB: Break Glass accounts are exempt from this control. For further guidance on Break Glass accounts see Emergency accounts (Break Glass accounts section).

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT use shared credentials to access accounts.

group.title: System user identification for shared accounts

control.title: 16.1.28.C.01. — System user identification for shared accounts

prop.name: topic
prop.value: System user identification for shared accounts

part.name: statement
part.p: If agencies choose to allow shared, non user-specific accounts they MUST ensure that an independent means of determining the identification of the system user is implemented and logged.

group.title: Methods for system user identification and authentication

control.title: 16.1.29.C.01. — Methods for system user identification and authentication

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Methods for system user identification and authentication

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT use a numerical password (or personal identification number) as the sole method of authenticating a system user to access a system.

control.title: 16.1.29.C.02. — Methods for system user identification and authentication

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Methods for system user identification and authentication

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use multi-factor authentication (MFA) when identifying and authenticating system users.

group.title: Centralisation of Identification and Authentication Management

control.title: 16.1.30.C.01. — Centralisation of Identification and Authentication Management

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Centralisation of Identification and Authentication Management

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD assess and determine the risk of centralised access management systems, including SSO, to safely manage integration into systems and when using FIM.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure adequate password policies are implemented and enforced across all systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST implement a password policy enforcing at least annual password changes on systems that have not implemented MFA or passwordless authentication.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST implement a password policy enforcing:

ul.li: A minimum password length of 16 characters (e.g four words).
Passwords must be long, strong and unique. This means passwords must be a minimum character length, and are a combination of unique random words, characters or numbers.
NB: no explicit complexity requirements are enforced (e.g. numbers or special characters), however passwords must be unique, or random and may include special characters and numbers to achieve this.

part.name: statement
part.p: To ensure security of systems are not weakened through authentication mechanisms, at a minimum, agencies MUST:

ul.li: apply MFA appropriately (refer to controls in Section 16.7);
ensure authentication secrets (including passwords) are securely stored;
remove knowledge-based questions from authentication process (eg, dog’s name, first school etc.);
new passwords are screened to reduce the likelihood of previously compromised passwords;
remove hints from authentication process; and
change passwords when a suspected or known compromise of an account has occurred.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT:

ul.li: allow predictable reset passwords;
store passwords in the clear on the system; and
reuse passwords when resetting multiple accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD consider the use of location-based factors in the authentication process, (e.g., Users must be at an expected location (city, country, IP address) and provide the correct credentials for the authentication to succeed).

part.name: statement
part.p: When creating password policies, agencies SHOULD consider implementing annual password changes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT allow storage of unprotected authentication information that grants system access, or decrypts an encrypted device, to be located on, or with the system or device, to which the authentication information grants access.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that system authentication data is protected when in transit on organisation networks or All-of-Government systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Password and other authentication secrets MUST be hashed before storage using an approved cryptographic protocol and algorithm. See Chapter 17 – Cryptography.

part.name: statement
part.p: Passwords and other authentication secrets MUST be stored securely including being:

ul.li: salted (32 bits or more),
salts should be unique to each password and should be randomly generated.
hashed (HMAC using SHA-2/3), and
“stretched” (such as PBKDF2 with at least:
600k iterations with internal hash function of HMAC-SHA-256; or
210k iterations with internal hash function of HMAC-SHA-512).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where systems contain NZEO or other nationalities releasability marked or protectively marked information, agencies MUST provide a mechanism that allows system users and processes to identify users who are foreign nationals, including seconded foreign nationals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using NZEO systems SHOULD ensure that identification includes specific nationality for all foreign nationals, including seconded foreign nationals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure system users provide sufficient evidence to prove they are the owner of the account when requesting a password reset for their system account or making changes to their multi-factor authenticators.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where passwords are not set by the account holder, agencies MUST use temporary passwords when resetting system user accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT use single factor authentication when changing users’ Multi-Factor Authentication details.

part.name: statement
part.p: Password managers provide no additional security to the sign-in password. Agencies using password managers MUST ensure sign-in passwords adhere to the password security policies used by the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using password managers SHOULD consider the use of MFA to access the password manager.

part.name: statement
part.p: When moving to passwordless authentication, agencies SHOULD carry out a risk assessment and evaluate passwordless authentication models to choose authentication mechanisms and factors that best fit the organisation’s security and authentication requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure authentication methods that are susceptible to replay attacks are disabled.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST disable LAN Manager for password authentication on workstations and servers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD develop and implement a policy to automatically logout and shutdown workstations after an appropriate time of inactivity. This includes invalidating any session tokens.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD:

ul.li: configure systems with a session or screen lock;
configure the lock to activate:
after a maximum of 10 minutes of system user inactivity; or
if manually activated by the system user;
configure the lock to completely conceal all information on the screen;
ensure that the screen is not turned off or enters a power saving state before the screen or session lock is activated;
have the system user reauthenticate to unlock the system; and
deny system users the ability to disable the locking mechanism.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: Record all successful and failed logon attempts;
lock system user accounts after three failed logon attempts;
use a temporary lock out feature to unlock system (max [] times);
have a system administrator reset locked accounts if [] times is superseded;
remove or suspend system user accounts as soon as possible when personnel no longer need access due to changing roles or leaving the organisation; and
remove or suspend inactive accounts after a specified number of days.
NB: Agencies can determine the risk of using a temporary lock out feature on their specific systems.
[] indicates the chosen 'value of times' an agency has decided to use for the temporary lock out feature.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD have a logon banner that requires a system user to acknowledge and accept their security responsibilities before access to the system is granted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD seek legal advice on the exact wording of logon banners.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agency logon banners SHOULD cover issues such as:

ul.li: the system’s classification;
access only being permitted to authorised system users;
the system user’s agreement to abide by relevant security policies;
the system user’s awareness of the possibility that system usage is being monitored;
the definition of acceptable use for the system; and
legal ramifications of violating the relevant policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST follow a defined process for developing an access control list, such as described in the table below.
Stage
Description
Establish groups of all system resources based on similar security objectives.
Determine the information owner for each group of resources.
Obtain agreement from system owners.
Establish groups encompassing all system users based on similar functions or security objectives.
Determine the group owner or manager for each group of system users.
Determine the degree of access to the resource for each system user group, incorporating the principal of least-privilege access.
Decide on the level of access for security administration, based on the internal security policy.
Identify any classification, protective markings, and releasability indicators (such as NZEO or compartmented information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST have authorisation of system users enforced by access controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST restrict access to compartmented information. Such restriction MUST be enforced by the system.

group.title: Access from foreign controlled systems and facilities

control.title: 16.2.7.C.01. — Access from foreign controlled systems and facilities

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Access from foreign controlled systems and facilities

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT allow access to NZEO information from systems and facilities not under the sole control of the government of New Zealand and New Zealand citizens.

control.title: 16.2.7.C.02. — Access from foreign controlled systems and facilities

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Access from foreign controlled systems and facilities

part.name: statement
part.p: Unless a multilateral or bilateral security agreement is in place, agencies SHOULD NOT allow access to classified information from systems and facilities not under the sole control of the government of New Zealand and New Zealand citizens.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: ensure strong change management practices are implemented;
ensure that the use of privileged accounts is controlled and accountable;
ensure that system administrators are assigned, and consistently use, an individual account for the performance of their administration tasks;
keep privileged accounts to a minimum; and
allow the use of privileged accounts for administrative work only.

group.title: Privileged system access by foreign nationals

control.title: 16.3.6.C.01. — Privileged system access by foreign nationals

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Privileged system access by foreign nationals

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT allow foreign nationals, including seconded foreign nationals, to have privileged access to systems that process, store or communicate NZEO information.

control.title: 16.3.6.C.02. — Privileged system access by foreign nationals

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Privileged system access by foreign nationals

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT allow foreign nationals, including seconded foreign nationals, to have privileged access to systems that process, store or communicate classified information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies involved in frequent transfers of data from another system to their system with a lesser classification SHOULD ensure at least one privileged user has a security clearance level commensurate the classification of the higher system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST establish a Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Within the context of agency operations, the agency’s PAM policy MUST define:

ul.li: a privileged account; and
privileged access.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST manage privileged accounts in accordance with the agency’s PAM policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST apply the Principle of Least Privilege when developing and implementing a Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use two-factor or Multi-Factor Authentication to allow access to privileged accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD consider the use of time bound revocation to privileged accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: As part of a Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy, agencies MUST establish and implement a strong approval and authorisation process before any privileged access credentials are issued.

part.name: statement
part.p: Privileged Access credentials MUST NOT be issued until approval has been formally granted.

group.title: Suspension and Revocation of Privileged Access Credentials

control.title: 16.4.39.C.01. — Suspension and Revocation of Privileged Access Credentials

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Suspension and Revocation of Privileged Access Credentials

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST establish robust credential suspension and revocation procedures as part of the agency’s Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy.

control.title: 16.4.39.C.02. — Suspension and Revocation of Privileged Access Credentials

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Suspension and Revocation of Privileged Access Credentials

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST investigate any indication of compromise or misuse of systems credentials or accounts.

group.title: Privileged Account, Rights and Credential Inventory

control.title: 16.4.40.C.01. — Privileged Account, Rights and Credential Inventory

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Privileged Account, Rights and Credential Inventory

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST create and maintain a comprehensive inventory of privileged accounts and the associated access rights and credentials.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST create, implement and maintain a robust system of continuous discovery, monitoring and review of privileged accounts and the access rights and credentials associated with those accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Privileged account monitoring systems MUST monitor and record:

ul.li: individual user activity, including exceptions such as out of hours access;
activity from unauthorised sources;
any unusual use patterns; and
any creation of unauthorised privileges access credentials.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST protect and limit access to activity and audit logs and records.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST develop and implement a response and remediation policy and procedure as part of an agency’s Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST implement a Privileged Access Management (PAM) policy training module as part of the agency’s overall user training and awareness requirement.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST authenticate each remote connection and user prior to permitting access to an agency system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD authenticate both the remote system user and device during the authentication process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT allow the use of remote privileged access from an untrusted domain, including logging in as an unprivileged system user and then escalating privileges.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD establish VPN connections for all remote access connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use Zero Trust principles alongside the use of VPN connections to enhance the security posture of the organisation. This should include removing the ability for a standard user to disable the VPN connection.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD determine a policy for the retention of system management logs.

part.name: statement
part.p: A system management log SHOULD record the following minimum information:

ul.li: all system start-up and shutdown;
all system changes;
user changes;
service, application, component or system failures;
maintenance activities;
backup and archival activities;
system recovery activities; and
special or out of hours activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST develop and document logging requirements covering:

ul.li: the logging facility, including:
log server availability requirements; and
the reliable delivery of log information to the log server;
the list of events associated with a system or software component to be logged; and
event log protection and archival requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD log the events listed in the table below for specific software components.
Software component
Events to log
Database
System user access to the database.
Attempted access that is denied.
Changes to system user roles or database rights.
Addition of new system users, especially privileged users.
Modifications to the data.
Modifications to the format or structure of the database.
Network/operating system
Successful and failed attempts to logon and logoff.
Changes to system administrator and system user accounts.
Failed attempts to access data and system resources.
Attempts to use special privileges.
Use of special privileges.
System user or group management.
Changes to the security policy.
Service failures and restarts.
System startup and shutdown.
Changes to system configuration data.
Access to sensitive data and processes.
Data import/export operations.
Web application
System user access to the Web application.
Attempted access that is denied.
System user access to the Web documents.
Search engine queries initiated by system users.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD log, at minimum, the following events for all software components:

ul.li: Any login activity or attempts; all privileged operations;
failed attempts to elevate privileges;
security related system alerts and failures;
all software updates and/or patching;
system user and group additions, deletions and modification to permissions; and
unauthorised or failed access attempts to systems and files identified as critical to the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: For each event identified as needing to be logged, agencies MUST ensure that the log facility records at least the following details, where applicable:

ul.li: date and time of the event;
relevant system user(s) or processes;
event description;
success or failure of the event;
event source (e.g. application name); and
IT equipment location/identification.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD establish an authoritative time source.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD synchronise all logging and audit trails with the time source to allow accurate time stamping of events.

part.name: statement
part.p: Event logs MUST be protected from:

ul.li: modification;
unauthorised access; and
whole or partial loss within the defined retention period.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that:

ul.li: systems are configured to save event logs to a separate secure log server; and
event log data is archived in a manner that maintains its integrity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Event logs MUST be archived and retained for an appropriate period as determined by the agency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Disposal or archiving of DNS, proxy, event, systems and other operational logs MUST be in accordance with the provisions of the relevant legislation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD seek advice and determine if their logs are subject to legislation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD retain DNS, proxy and event logs for a minimum of 12 months.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies should prioritise their log retention requirements based on the risks surrounding their most sensitive systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST develop and document event log audit requirements covering:

ul.li: the scope of audits;
the audit schedule;
action to be taken when violations are detected;
reporting requirements; and
roles and specific responsibilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD have a monitoring solution implemented that enables detection of incidents as they occur so that appropriate responses can be taken in adequate timeframes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD have systems available for processing system event logs to identify and correlate events which indicate behavioural anomalies or potential security compromise in the systems, in a near real-time manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST undertake a risk analysis before designing and implementing MFA.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an agency has external facing systems, cloud-based services, or is authenticating to third-party services services, they MUST:

ul.li: require MFA for all user accounts; and
implement a secure, multi-factor process to allow entities to reset their standard user credentials.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where an agency has implemented MFA they MUST:

ul.li: require MFA for administrative or other high privileged users; and
implement a secure, multi-factor process to allow entities to reset their standard user credentials.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST implement MFA on all user accounts with remote access to organisational resources.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement MFA on all user accounts with access to organisational resources.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where agencies have implemented MFA, they SHOULD implement phishing-resistant MFA on administration accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use phishing-resistant MFA when authenticating users to systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The design of an agency MFA SHOULD include consideration of:

ul.li: Risk identification;
Level of security and access control appropriate for each aspect of an organisation’s information systems (data, devices, equipment, storage, cloud, etc.)
A formal authorisation process for user system access and entitlements;
Logging, monitoring and reporting of activity;
Review of logs for orphaned accounts and inappropriate user access including unsuccessful authentication;
Identification of error and anomalies which may indicate inappropriate or malicious activity;
Incident response;
Remediation of errors;
Suspension and/or revocation of access rights where policy violations occur;
Capacity planning.

part.name: statement
part.p: The design of an organisations MFA system SHOULD be integrated with the agency’s Information Security Policy, the agency’s Privileged Access Management (PAM) Policy, and any additional agency password policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: When agencies’ implement MFA they MUST ensure users have an understanding of the risks, and include appropriate usage and safeguards for MFA in the organisation’s user training and awareness programmes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using cryptographic functionality within a product to protect the confidentiality, authentication, non-repudiation or integrity of information, MUST ensure that the product has completed a cryptographic evaluation recognised by the GCSB.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic products SHOULD provide a means of data recovery to allow for recovery of data in circumstances where the encryption key is unavailable due to loss, damage or failure.

group.title: Reducing storage and physical transfer requirements

control.title: 17.1.53.C.01. — Reducing storage and physical transfer requirements

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Reducing storage and physical transfer requirements

part.name: statement
part.p: Encryption used to reduce storage or physical handling protection requirements MUST be an approved cryptographic algorithm in an EAL2 (or higher) encryption product.

control.title: 17.1.53.C.04. — Reducing storage and physical transfer requirements

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Reducing storage and physical transfer requirements

part.name: statement
part.p: If an agency wishes to use encryption to reduce the storage or physical transfer requirements for IT equipment or media that contains classified information, they SHOULD use:

ul.li: full disk encryption; or
partial disk encryption where the access control will allow writing ONLY to the encrypted partition holding the classified information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use an Approved Cryptographic Algorithm to protect NZEO information when at rest on a system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information or systems classified RESTRICTED or SENSITIVE MUST be encrypted with an Approved Cryptographic Algorithm and Protocol if information is transmitted or systems are communicating over insecure or unprotected networks, such as the Internet, public networks or non-agency controlled networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST encrypt aggregated agency data using an approved algorithm and protocol over insecure or unprotected networks such as the Internet, public infrastructure or non-agency controlled networks when the compromise of the aggregated data would present a significant impact to the agency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD encrypt agency data using an approved algorithm and protocol if they wish to communicate over insecure or unprotected networks such as the Internet, public networks or non-agency controlled networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: When IT equipment storing encrypted information is turned on and authenticated, it MUST be treated as per the original classification of the information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST consult the GCSB for further advice on the powered off status and treatment of specific software, systems and IT equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: In addition to any encryption already in place for communication mediums, agencies MUST use an Approved Cryptographic Protocol and Algorithm to protect NZEO information when in transit.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD establish cryptoperiods for all keys and cryptographic implementations in their systems and operations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use risk assessment techniques and guidance to establish cryptoperiods.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using HACE MUST consult the GCSB for key management requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST ensure that only Approved Cryptographic Algorithms can be used when using an unevaluated product that implements a combination of approved and non-approved Cryptographic Algorithms.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use ECDH and ECDSA for all new systems, version upgrades and major system modifications.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using DH, for the approved use of agreeing on encryption session keys, MUST use a modulus of at least 3072 bits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Devices which are NOT capable of implementing required key lengths MUST be reconfigured with the longest feasible key length as a matter of urgency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Devices which are NOT capable of implementing required key lengths MUST be scheduled for replacement as a matter of urgency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using DSA, for the approved use of digital signatures, MUST use a modulus of at least 1024 bits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using ECDH, for the approved use of agreeing on encryption session keys, MUST implement the curve P-384 (prime moduli).

part.name: statement
part.p: All VPN’s using an ECDH key length less than 384 MUST replace all Pre-Shared Keys with keys of at least 384 bits, as soon as possible.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using ECDSA, for the approved use of digital signatures, MUST implement the curve P-384 (prime moduli).

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using RSA, for the approved use of digital signatures and passing encryption session keys or similar keys, MUST use a modulus of at least 3072 bits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using RSA, for the approved use of digital signatures and passing encryption session keys or similar keys, MUST ensure that the public keys used for passing encrypted session keys are different to the keys used for digital signatures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using RSA, for the approved use of digital signatures and passing encryption session keys or similar keys, SHOULD use a modulus of at least 4096 bits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using RSA keys within internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure certificates MUST use a modulus of at least 2048 bits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use the SHA-2 family for new systems. Use of SHA-1 is permitted ONLY for legacy systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST use a minimum of SHA-384 when using hashing algorithms to provide integrity protection for information classified as RESTRICTED/SENSITIVE or above.

part.name: statement
part.p: In all other cases when information requires integrity protection using hashing algorithms, Agencies MUST use a minimum of SHA-256.

part.name: statement
part.p: Memorised secrets such as passwords MUST be stored in a form that is resistant to offline attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Memorised secrets such as passwords SHOULD be salted and hashed using a suitable one-way key derivation function. See 17.2.14.

part.name: statement
part.p: The salt SHOULD be at least 32 bits in length, be chosen arbitrarily, and each instance is unique so as to minimise salt value collisions among stored hashes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using approved symmetric encryption algorithms (e.g. AES) SHOULD NOT use Electronic Code Book (ECB) mode.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using a product that implements an Approved Cryptographic Protocol MUST ensure that only Approved Cryptographic Protocols can be used.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use the current version of TLS (version 1.3).

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT use any version of SSL.

part.name: statement

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use public key-based authentication before using password-based authentication.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies that allow password authentication SHOULD use techniques to block brute force attacks against the password.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use parameter checking when using the ‘forced command’ option.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies that use logins without a password for automated purposes SHOULD disable:

ul.li: access from IP addresses that do not need access;
port forwarding;
agent credential forwarding;
X11 display remoting; and
console access.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies that use remote access without the use of a password SHOULD use the ‘forced command’ option to specify what command is executed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies that use SSH-agent or other similar key caching programs SHOULD:

ul.li: only use the software on workstation and servers with screenlocks;
ensure that the key cache expires within four hours of inactivity; and
ensure that agent credential forwarding is used when multiple SSH traversal is needed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure that the latest implementation of SSH software is being used. Older versions contain known vulnerabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Decommissioning of faulty or redundant equipment MUST comply with media sanitisation requirements described in Chapter 12 – Product Security.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST NOT allow versions of S/MIME earlier than 3.0 to be used.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST immediately revoke key pairs when a private certificate is suspected of being compromised or leaves the control of the agency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use tunnel mode for IPSec connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies choosing to use transport mode SHOULD additionally use an IP tunnel for IPSec connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use the ESP protocol for IPSec connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using ISAKMP SHOULD disable aggressive mode for IKE.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use a security association lifetime of four hours or 14400 seconds, or less.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use HMAC-SHA256, HMAC-SHA384 or HMAC-SHA512 as the HMAC algorithm.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use the largest modulus size available for the DH exchange.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use Perfect Forward Secrecy for IPSec connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD disable the use of XAUTH for IPSec connections using IKEv1.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD assess the risks associated around key ownership, possession, and control against their own security and business requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD develop a KMP when they have implemented a cryptographic system using commercial grade cryptographic equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The level of detail included in a KMP MUST be consistent with the criticality and classification of the information to be protected.

part.name: statement
part.p: The table below describes the minimum contents which SHOULD be documented in the KMP.
Topic
Content
Objectives
Objectives of the cryptographic system and KMP, including organisational aims.
Refer to relevant NZCSIs.
System description
The environment.
Maximum classification of information protected.
Topology diagram(s) and description of the cryptographic system topology including data flows.
The use of keys.
Key algorithm.
Key length.
Key lifetime.
Roles and administrative responsibilities
Documents roles and responsibilities, including, if relevant, the COMSEC custodian, cryptographic systems administrator, record keeper, cloud service provider, and auditor.
Accounting
How accounting will be undertaken for the cryptographic system.
What records will be maintained.
How records will be audited.
Classification
Classification of the cryptographic system hardware.
Classification of cryptographic system software.
Classification of the cryptographic system documentation.
Information security incidents
A description of the conditions under which compromise of key material should be declared.
References to procedures to be followed when reporting and dealing with information security incidents.
Key management
Who generates keys.
How keys are delivered.
How keys are received.
Key distribution, including local, remote and central.
How keys are installed.
How keys are transferred.
How keys are stored.
How keys are recovered.
How keys are revoked.
How keys are destroyed.
Each time key information or material is accessed, details are captured in logs.
Approved access lists to cryptographic keys.
Maintenance
Maintaining the cryptographic system software and hardware.
Destroying equipment and media.
References
Vendor documentation.
Related policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD be able to readily account for all transactions relating to cryptographic system material including identifying hardware and all software versions issued with the equipment and materials, including date and place of issue.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST conduct audits using two personnel with cryptographic system administrator access.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD conduct audits of cryptographic system material:

ul.li: on handover/takeover of administrative responsibility for the cryptographic system;
on change of personnel with access to the cryptographic system; and
at least annually.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD perform audits to:

ul.li: account for all cryptographic system material; and
confirm that agreed security measures documented in the KMP are being followed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST hold and maintain an access register that records cryptographic system information such as:

ul.li: details of personnel with system administrator access;
details of those whose system administrator access was withdrawn;
details of system documents;
accounting activities; and
audit activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Before personnel are granted cryptographic system administrator access, agencies MUST ensure that they have:

ul.li: a demonstrated need for access;
read and agreed to comply with the relevant Key Management Policy and Plan (KMP) for the cryptographic system they are using;
a security clearance at least equal to the highest classification of information processed by the cryptographic system;
agreed to protect the authentication information for the cryptographic system at the highest classification of information it secures;
agreed not to share authentication information for the cryptographic system without approval;
agreed to be responsible for all actions under their accounts;
agreed to report all potentially security related problems to the GCSB; and
ensure relevant staff have received appropriate training.

part.p: Cryptographic system equipment SHOULD be stored in a room that meets the requirements for a server room of an appropriate level based on the classification of information the cryptographic system processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST comply with NZCSI when using HACE.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST perform a security risk assessment before providing network documentation to a third party, such as a commercial provider or contractor.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network documentation provided to a third party, such as to a commercial provider or contractor, MUST contain only the information necessary for them to undertake their contractual services and functions, consistent with the need-to-know principle.

part.name: statement
part.p: Detailed network configuration information MUST NOT be published in tender documentation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security aspects SHOULD be considered when determining the classification level of systems and network documentation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD keep the network configuration under the control of a network management authority.

part.name: statement
part.p: All changes to the configuration SHOULD be documented and approved through a formal change control process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD regularly review their network configuration to ensure that it conforms to the documented network configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD deploy an automated tool that compares the running configuration of network devices against the documented configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: For each network an agency manages they MUST have:

ul.li: a high-level diagram showing all connections and gateways into the network; and
a network diagram showing all communications equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: An agency’s network diagrams SHOULD:

ul.li: be updated as network changes are made; and
include a ‘Current as at [date]’ statement on each page.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement network access controls on all networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement protection measures to minimise the risk of unauthorised access to network management traffic on a network.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD NOT use SNMP unless a specific requirement exists.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD implement SNMPv3 where a specific SNMP requirement exists.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD change all default community strings in SNMP implementations.

part.name: statement
part.p: SNMP access SHOULD be configured as read-only.

part.name: statement
part.p: Devices MUST NOT be configured to remember and automatically connect to any wireless networks that they have previously connected to.

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless auto-connect functionality on devices SHOULD be disabled, preferably by a hardware switch, whenever connected to a fixed network.

control.title: 18.2.6.C.01. — Providing wireless communications for public access

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Providing wireless communications for public access

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies deploying a wireless network for public access MUST separate it from any other agency networks; including BYOD networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: All wireless access points used for government wireless networks MUST be Wi-Fi Alliance certified.

part.name: statement
part.p: EAP-TLS, PEAP-EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS or PEAP MUST be used on wireless networks to perform mutual authentication.

part.name: statement
part.p: Supplicants, authenticators and the authentication server used in wireless networks SHOULD have completed an appropriate product evaluation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST generate certificates using a certificate authority product or hardware security module that has completed an appropriate product evaluation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The certificates for both a device and user accessing a wireless network MUST NOT be stored on the same device.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use unique certificates for both devices and users accessing a wireless network.

part.name: statement
part.p: Certificates for users accessing wireless networks SHOULD be issued on smart cards with access PINs and not stored with a device when not in use.

part.name: statement
part.p: Certificates stored on devices accessing wireless networks SHOULD be protected by implementing full disk encryption on the devices.

changing settings; and

group.title: Developing a denial of service response plan

control.title: 18.3.18.C.01. — Developing a denial of service response plan

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Developing a denial of service response plan

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD develop a Denial of Service response plan including:

ul.li: how to identify the precursors and other signs of DoS;
how to diagnose the incident or attack type and attack method;
how to diagnose the source of the DoS;
what actions can be taken to clear the DoS;
how communications can be maintained during a DoS; and
report the incident.

group.title: Content of a Denial of Service (DoS) response plan

control.title: 18.3.19.C.01. — Content of a Denial of Service (DoS) response plan

prop.name: topic
prop.value: Content of a Denial of Service (DoS) response plan

part.name: statement
part.p: A Denial of Service response plan SHOULD include monitoring and use of:

ul.li: router and switch logging and flow data;
packet captures;
proxy and call manager logs and access control lists;
VTC and IPT aware firewalls and voice gateways;
network redundancy;
load balancing;
PSTN failover; and
alternative communication paths.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD develop, implement and maintain an intrusion detection strategy that includes:

ul.li: appropriate intrusion detection mechanisms, including network-based IDS/IPSs and host-based IDS/IPSs as necessary;
the audit analysis of event logs, including IDS/IPS logs;
a periodic audit of intrusion detection procedures;
information security awareness and training programs; and
a documented IRP.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD ensure sufficient resources are provided for the maintenance and monitoring of IDS/IPS.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD deploy IDS/IPSs in all gateways between the agency’s networks and unsecure public networks or BYOD wireless networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD deploy IDS/IPSs at all gateways between the agency’s networks and any network not managed by the agency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD locate IDS/IPSs within the gateway environment, immediately inside the outermost firewall.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST select IDS / IPS that monitor uncharacteristic and suspicious activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: When signature-based intrusion detection is used, agencies MUST keep the signatures and system patching up to date.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies MUST:

ul.li: develop and maintain a set of policies and procedures covering how to:
minimise the likelihood of malicious code being introduced into a system;
prevent all unauthorised code from executing on an agency network;
detect any malicious code installed on a system;
make their system users aware of the agency’s policies and procedures; and
ensure that all instances of detected malicious code outbreaks are handled according to established procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: In addition to agency defined configuration requirements, agencies SHOULD ensure that IDS/IPSs located inside a firewall are configured to generate a log entry, and an alert, for any information flows that contravene any rule within the firewall rule set.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD test IDS/IPSs rule sets prior to implementation to ensure that they perform as expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: If a firewall is configured to block all traffic on a particular range of port numbers, the IDP/IPSs SHOULD inspect traffic for these port numbers and generate an alert if they are detected.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD deploy tools for:

ul.li: the management and archive of security event information; and
the correlation of suspicious events or events of interest across all agency networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD install host-based IDS/IPSs on authentication, DNS, email, Web and other high value servers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD use:

ul.li: filters to block unwanted content and exploits against applications that cannot be patched;
settings within the applications to disable unwanted functionality; and
digital signatures to restrict active content to trusted sources only.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies not using IPv6, but which have deployed dual-stack network devices and ICT equipment that supports IPv6, MUST disable the IPv6 functionality, unless that functionality is required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies using IPv6 MUST conduct a security risk assessment on risks that could be introduced as a result of running a dual stack environment or transitioning completely to IPv6.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies implementing a dual stack or wholly IPv6 network or environment MUST re-accredit their networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: IPv6 tunnelling MUST be disabled on all network devices, unless explicitly required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Dynamically assigned IPv6 addresses SHOULD be configured with DHCPv6 in a stateful manner and with lease information logged and logs stored in a centralised logging facility.

part.name: statement
part.p: Any network defence elements and devices MUST be IPv6 aware.

part.name: statement
part.p: New network devices, including firewalls, IDS and IPS, MUST be IPv6 capable.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agencies SHOULD consider the use of DNSSEC.
